Other signals, including hormones from the gut, help the pancreas to judge how much is needed.

Insulin works rather like a key, signalling to the cells of the muscles, the liver and the fat tissue that they should open up and take glucose in from the blood. Once the sugar has been absorbed, the cells burn it for immediate energy or put it aside, and the level in the bloodstream falls back toward normal. In a healthy body this adjustment happens all day long without anyone noticing it.

In a healthy body the level of sugar in the blood rises after a meal, reaches its peak in about an hour, and then drifts back toward normal over the next couple of hours. Ines drew this as a gentle hill on a napkin and said that the shape of the hill, its height and its slope, differs from meal to meal and from person to person. It is a rhythm, not a fault, and the body handles it dozens of times a week without our noticing.

The liver and the muscles can pack away extra glucose in a compact form called glycogen, rather like stacking boxes in a warehouse. Between meals, and especially overnight, the liver breaks some of this store down and releases it into the blood, so the brain is never left without fuel. Noor, who rose at three every morning, was relieved to learn that her body had been quietly managing without breakfast for years.

Insulin does more than lower blood sugar, for it also encourages fat cells to take up and store extra energy and slows the release of fat from those stores. After a meal, then, the body is in a saving mood, putting fuel in the larder, and between meals it is in a spending mood as insulin falls. There is nothing sinister in this, Ines said, because storing energy is exactly what a healthy body is meant to do.

Insulin has a partner called glucagon, which is also made in the pancreas and which does very nearly the opposite. When blood sugar falls too low, glucagon rises and tells the liver to release some of its stored glucose, so the level never drops further than it should. Together the two hormones work like a pair of hands on a tap, one opening and one closing, keeping the flow even.

Noor was amazed to discover that her body had been balancing her blood sugar all her life without so much as a request. Ines agreed that the system is remarkably clever, but she added that it has limits, and that in some people it does not work as it should. That, she said, was the subject for tomorrow, and she would be careful not to frighten anyone.

Ines set two meals on the garden table, a white roll with a glass of fruit juice and a bowl of lentil soup, and asked Noor which would raise her blood sugar faster. The roll and juice would, of course, because their sugars are quickly absorbed, whereas the lentils are digested more slowly and release their glucose over a longer time. Scientists describe this difference with a scale called the glycaemic index, though it is only one rough guide among several.

Sugary drinks and highly refined foods tend to produce a tall, steep hill of blood sugar, because there is almost nothing in them to slow the digestion. Whole grains, beans and many vegetables usually produce a lower and longer hill, since their structure holds the sugars back and releases them gradually. Ines stressed that both kinds of food have their place, and that nothing was being forbidden.

Fibre is the part of plant foods that our own digestive enzymes cannot break down, and it does several quiet jobs on its way through the body. It slows the rate at which sugars enter the blood, adds bulk that helps the gut to move and feeds the trillions of bacteria that live in the large intestine. It is also one of the reasons why a bowl of oats feels so different from a sugary cereal.

When protein, fat or fibre are eaten along with carbohydrate, the rise in blood sugar usually becomes slower and smaller, because the stomach empties more gradually. A few small studies even suggest that eating vegetables before bread may flatten the hill further, though the evidence is limited and the effect varies from one person to another. Ines was cautious about turning such findings into rules, and she hoped Noor would be too.

Noor admitted that she often felt tired and hungry an hour after something sweet, and Ines said that many people describe exactly this experience. Scientists have not agreed on a single explanation, since the supposed crash in blood sugar turns out to be less common in healthy people than the popular stories suggest. What is clear is that the feeling is real, even if its cause is still being argued over.

For two days Noor ate a roll with juice at lunchtime, and for the next two she ate lentils with a little bread, writing down how she felt afterwards. She seemed steadier after the lentils, but Ines pointed out that a few days in one person's life prove very little, since sleep, weather and mood all play their part. Even so, she said, careful noticing is a fine way to begin asking better questions.

Ines explained, as simply as she could, that in type 1 diabetes the immune system damages the pancreas cells that make insulin, so the body produces almost none. People with this condition need to take insulin every day, through injections or a small pump, and they learn to match the dose to what they eat and how active they are. It is not caused by eating sugar or by anything the person did, and it is certainly not anybody's fault.

In type 2 diabetes the cells respond less well to insulin, so the pancreas has to make more of it to do the same job, and in time it may struggle to keep up. The causes are many and tangled, among them genes, age, body weight, activity and sleep, and doctors have a growing range of ways to treat it. Ines was firm that treatment starts with a conversation and a test, never with blame.

Ines remembered patients she had cared for who were blamed, by strangers and sometimes by themselves, for a condition they had never chosen. Shame, she said, keeps people away from their doctors, delays tests and makes treatment harder, which is the opposite of what anyone needs. Noor listened quietly, thinking of the times she had made unkind jokes about her own appetite.

Hunger alone cannot tell anyone what their blood sugar is doing, because only a simple test at a doctor's or a pharmacy can show that. Ines said that very strong thirst, needing the toilet unusually often, unexplained weight loss or constant tiredness are all reasons to see a doctor promptly, and that nobody should wait to feel ashamed first. Noor, though she had none of these signs, wrote the number of her own doctor's surgery on the back of her hand.

On Sunday morning Noor sat at Ines's kitchen table and cracked two eggs into a hot pan while a bowl of warm beans steamed beside it. Ines explained that, calorie for calorie, protein tends to keep people feeling full for longer than fat or carbohydrate does, at least in short studies. Noor, who usually ate a roll standing up before dawn, wrote that sentence in her notebook and underlined it twice.

Protein seems to switch on the fullness hormones of the gut more strongly than some other foods do, and it also takes the body a little more energy to digest. Researchers do not agree on how much each effect matters, and the size of the difference varies between studies and between people. Ines described it as a modest advantage, not a miracle, and Noor was glad to be told so.

Ines pointed out that the gut is not only a tube for digestion but also one of the largest hormone-producing systems in the body. Its lining holds special cells that sense the nutrients passing by, almost as if they were tasting them, and they respond by releasing hormones into the blood. Noor looked down at her empty plate and felt something close to respect for the long, patient machinery that had just dealt with her breakfast.

When fat and protein reach the small intestine, special cells release a hormone with the clumsy name cholecystokinin, usually shortened to CCK. It slows the emptying of the stomach, prompts the gallbladder to squeeze out bile for digesting fat and sends a message to the brain that food has arrived. Ines promised, with a perfectly straight face, that she would not be testing Noor on the spelling of that particular word later in the evening.

Further along the gut, cells in the lower small intestine and the colon release peptide YY, which scientists usually abbreviate to PYY. Its level climbs after a meal and stays raised for several hours, and in studies it tends to reduce appetite and the wish to eat more. Together with CCK, it forms part of what Ines liked to call the gut's quiet braking system, a set of signals that slow eating without any conscious effort.

The vagus nerve is a long and wandering cable that runs from the base of the brain down through the chest to the gut, and it carries news in both directions. Some hormones, CCK among them, work partly by stimulating the endings of this nerve, so the body uses hormones and nerves together instead of choosing one. Noor remembered the napkin from the first night and added another arrow to it.

Ines cooked a big pot of bean stew and talked, while it simmered, about the bacteria that live in the human gut. When they ferment fibre they produce substances that may influence the release of fullness hormones, and some research in animals and people points that way. She was careful to say that this science is young and that nobody yet knows how much it matters in daily life.

After the stew Noor felt comfortably full and yet found herself eyeing the cake on the sideboard with unmistakable longing. Ines laughed and explained that fullness and the wish for something delicious are separate things, handled by different systems in the brain. The first tells us the body has had enough, whereas the second belongs to the reward system, which they would meet in a few days.

Ines said that two people can eat exactly the same breakfast and feel quite different afterwards, because bodies, habits and even gut bacteria vary. Some feel pleasantly full on porridge until lunchtime, while others are hungry again within the hour. It is one more reason, she added, to be suspicious of a rule that claims to suit everybody.

Noor summed up the week by saying that the gut hormones act as brakes after a meal, slowing the stomach and telling the brain that fuel has arrived. Ines agreed, and added that the brakes do not work identically in everyone and that they take time to take hold. That, she said, would be the subject of the next few evenings, and it involved a stomach that stretches like a balloon.

Between customers on a busy Tuesday, Noor swallowed her lunch in four minutes flat, standing at the counter with one eye on the door. Half an hour later she was hungry again, and a little cross about it, since she knew she had eaten a perfectly good meal. That evening Ines asked her to describe how fast she had eaten, and the answer explained a great deal.

The stomach is a muscular, stretchy bag, quite small when empty, but able to expand to hold well over a litre of food and drink. Its lining is full of tiny sensors that notice how far the wall is stretched, and they report to the brain as the meal goes in. Ines compared it to a balloon that tells you, politely, when it is nearly full.

When the stomach wall stretches, nerve endings in it send a message up the vagus nerve to the brain, and this is one of the ways the body learns that it has eaten enough. The message does not work alone, since it joins the chemical signals coming from the gut and from the blood. Ines said that no single measurement tells the brain when to stop, and that is both a weakness and a strength.

The signals of fullness do not arrive all at once, since hormones have to be released, carried in the blood and read by the brain. People often say that twenty minutes is needed for this to happen, but Ines called the figure a rough guide and not a rule, because the timing differs between people and meals. What matters, she said, is the principle that the brain is slower than the fork.

Some studies have found that people who eat slowly consume a little less during the meal and report feeling fuller afterwards. The effect is modest, though, and not every study agrees, so Ines suggested that Noor treat the idea as a small experiment instead of a promise. If it did not help, she said, nothing was lost, and Noor would at least have eaten one lunch properly.

At the garden table Noor tried putting her fork down between mouthfuls and chewing each one properly, which felt faintly ridiculous at first. Soon, however, she noticed the sweetness of the carrots in her soup and the pepper behind it, flavours she had been swallowing unnoticed for months. She finished the bowl feeling calmer than usual, although she was honest enough to admit that she had also been looking forward to the conversation.

After a meal the gut releases a hormone called GLP-1, which helps the pancreas to release insulin when blood sugar is high, slows the emptying of the stomach and tells the brain that food has arrived. The body breaks it down within minutes, so its messages are brief, although they are repeated with every bite. Ines said that of all the gut hormones, it had become the most closely watched by scientists.

Scientists have developed medicines that imitate GLP-1 and last far longer in the body than the natural hormone does. They were first used for type 2 diabetes, and some are now also approved in many countries to help with weight management, always under a doctor's supervision. Noor asked whether she should try one, and Ines smiled and said that this was a question for her own doctor and not for a neighbour.

These medicines can cause side effects, such as nausea and stomach upset, and they are not suitable for everyone, so a doctor must weigh the risks and benefits for each person. Studies also suggest that in many people weight returns after the medicine is stopped, which supports the idea that the body defends its usual range. Ines wanted Noor to know that the science here is moving fast and that today's facts may be updated.

Ines said that medicines are tools and not a judgement on anybody's character, and that no one should feel proud or ashamed of using one. Any decision about taking them belongs to a person and their doctor, and strangers on the internet or neighbours with tea have no business interfering. Noor raised her cup to that, and they sat in the cooling air until the first bats appeared.

On Saturday a queue stretched out of the bakery door and along the pavement, and Noor served customers without a pause until the afternoon was nearly gone. Her lunch box stayed closed under the counter, forgotten beside a tray of cooling loaves, while the clock moved quietly past two and then past three. She did not notice any of it until the rush finally thinned, and then the hunger arrived all at once, like a wave breaking.

By four o'clock Noor felt weak, shaky and strangely tearful, and when Tariq dropped a tray she snapped at him in a way she would never normally have done. She was horrified at herself, for he was only seventeen and trying his best, and she apologised at once. Ines, who had come in for a loaf, watched the scene with sympathy and said nothing.

Noor grabbed a biscuit, then another, then a third, eating them so fast that she barely tasted any of them. Afterwards she felt irritated with herself, as though she had failed a test she had never known she was taking. Only later did Ines point out that this was precisely what a body does after a long fast, and that the failure, if any, belonged to biology and not to Noor.

Ines explained that when a person has gone a long time without food, ghrelin is high, and the brain's reward system pays closer attention to anything edible. Calm decisions become harder at such moments, because the brain is far more interested in fast fuel than in careful planning. Some small studies even suggest that hunger can sharpen irritability, which would explain the rather unfortunate word hangry.

Ines was quick to say that skipping a meal is not a sin, and that some people feel perfectly well on two meals a day. For Noor, however, a long gap seemed to produce a violent swing in hunger followed by a feast she did not enjoy, and that was a useful thing to have learned about herself. The aim, she said, was knowledge about your own body and not a rule imposed by someone else.

Noor got up at three every morning to light the ovens, and on most nights she managed only five or six hours of sleep. She had always assumed that tiredness and hunger were separate troubles, but lately she had begun to wonder whether they might be connected. It was a question Ines was delighted to answer, since sleep was one of her favourite subjects.

In some careful laboratory studies, people who had slept very little showed higher ghrelin and lower leptin the following day, and they reported feeling hungrier. The results are not identical from one study to the next, however, and the effects were fairly small, so it would be wrong to say that sleep explains everything. Even so, the pattern appeared often enough across different studies that researchers have begun to take the link between sleep and appetite seriously.

In laboratory studies, even a few nights of short sleep were enough to make the body respond less well to insulin, which means blood sugar stays higher for longer. Brain scans also suggest that tired people find rich, energy-dense food more tempting, although much of the evidence comes from small studies that need repeating. Ines emphasised that none of this was meant to make anyone anxious about a bad night.

Noor could not change the hours that bakers keep, but she and Ines made a list of small and realistic adjustments. She would go to bed a little earlier, put her phone away for the last half hour before sleep, and take a short nap in the quiet part of the afternoon. Ines said that nothing on the list was a cure, only a way of being a little kinder to a tired body.

After a full eight hours of sleep on Sunday, Noor noticed that she did not feel the usual pull toward a mid-morning snack, and she mentioned it to Ines with a triumphant smile. Ines was pleased, but she reminded her that one good weekend proves nothing, since a hundred small things differ from one day to the next. It was, she said, a promising clue and not a verdict, and a good reason to keep watching her own sleep without any drama.

In the week before a big holiday, orders poured in until the bakery was crowded from the moment it opened until the last loaf was sold. Noor felt her heart race and her hands tremble, and although she was far too busy to think about it, she could not help wondering what was happening inside her. That evening in the garden, Ines said that the answer was a pair of hormones with a very old job.

Ines explained that two small glands, called the adrenal glands, sit on top of the kidneys like caps, and that they release the body's main stress hormones. Adrenaline is released within seconds and prepares the body for action, whereas cortisol follows more slowly and keeps the effort going. Both are far older than any bakery, and both evolved to help animals cope with real danger.

After a sudden fright, adrenaline floods the blood, the heart speeds up and the body prepares itself to fight or to run. In that moment appetite usually vanishes, since digesting a meal is not a priority when one may need to escape, and many people have felt this before an exam or a speech. The effect is temporary, however, and hunger commonly returns once the moment has passed.

When stress continues for weeks, cortisol stays raised, and for many people appetite increases and the craving for rich, sweet or salty food grows. Others react in exactly the opposite way and lose their appetite, so the effect is far from the same for everyone. Ines said that Noor's late-night toast during the holiday rush was a very common and very human response.

Cortisol follows a daily rhythm that is set by the body's internal clock, rising sharply in the early morning, when it helps us to wake and get moving, and falling slowly through the day. By the middle of the night it is at its lowest point, which is one reason why sleep is a time of repair. Noor, who was up with the ovens at three, wondered what her own rhythm looked like.

Ines wanted Noor to understand that cortisol is not a villain, whatever the magazines may say. It raises blood sugar when the body needs energy, helps to control inflammation and keeps blood pressure steady, and a life without it would be impossible. Trouble arises only when its levels are too high or too low for too long, which is rare and which a doctor can test for.

A few rare medical conditions cause the body to make far too much cortisol, and they need proper tests and treatment from a doctor. Ordinary stress, even when it is heavy, is a different matter, and the popular claims about a so-called cortisol belly are mostly exaggerated. Ines said she would rather Noor read a good book than a bad magazine on the subject.

Eating can soothe a worried mind for a short while, and the brain remembers the lesson and repeats it the next time stress appears. That is why so many people reach for comfort food when they are under pressure, and why it is a learned habit, not a flaw of character. Ines said that the kind response is to understand the habit and to add other comforts alongside it.

Ines said that a short walk, a few slow breaths or a talk with a friend may help to ease stress, and that research supports many such simple things. She added that nothing works for everybody, so the sensible course was to try a few and keep whatever helped. Noor decided to start with the cheapest of the lot, which was standing in the yard for five minutes.

In the middle of the rush, Noor stepped into the yard for five minutes, leaned against the fence and breathed slowly while the sun warmed her face. When she went back inside she found, to her surprise, that the biscuit she had been eyeing no longer seemed so urgent. It was only one afternoon, and she told Ines so, but it felt like the first small step in a long and interesting experiment.

One evening Noor found herself on the sofa with a generous slice of cake on her knee and the television murmuring in front of her. She was not in the least hungry, having eaten a proper supper an hour before, and she sat there wondering why her hand kept travelling to the plate. It was, she decided, a puzzle well worth bringing to Ines when she next saw her over the garden wall.

Ines explained that people eat for two broad reasons, because the body needs energy and because food gives pleasure, and she said that scientists sometimes label these homeostatic and hedonic eating. In real life the two are mixed together all the time, so a single slice of cake can be a little of each. Noticing which one is speaking, she added, is a skill that can be learned.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger that nerve cells use to talk to each other, and it is often called the pleasure chemical in popular articles. That label is misleading, since the research links it more closely to motivation, the pull of wanting something, than to the enjoyment of having it. Ines said it was better to think of dopamine as the part of the brain that says, go and get that.

Researchers have shown that wanting and liking depend on partly different systems in the brain, which means that a person can crave something intensely and then enjoy it only a little. Noor recognised this at once, for she could remember eating plenty of biscuits that she had badly wanted and scarcely tasted. The distinction, Ines said, explains a good deal about why we sometimes eat on autopilot.

Cues such as a smell, a shop window, an advertisement or a certain time of day can set off wanting, even when the body has already had enough. The brain learns to link them with food, and the response fires up automatically, sometimes before the person is aware of it. Ines said that advertisers know this very well and design their work around it.

On her way home Noor passed another bakery with a poster of a glossy doughnut in its window, and she felt a sudden, sharp pull that had nothing to do with her stomach. She had to smile, because she made doughnuts herself and knew exactly how they were put together. Knowing the trick, it seemed, did not make the pull go away, but it did make it easier to observe.

Foods that combine plenty of sugar with plenty of fat seem to be especially rewarding to the brain, and experiments suggest that people find them harder to stop eating. Such combinations are rare in nature, but they are everywhere in cakes, pastries and snack aisles, which is a little awkward for a baker to admit. Ines laughed and said that Noor was not to feel guilty for being good at her job.

Dopamine is by no means the only chemical involved, and the picture grows more complicated every year. Endorphins, which the body also releases during exercise, laughter and certain foods, help to create feelings of comfort and pleasure, and several other messengers join in as well. Ines said that the brain's reward system was less a single switch than an orchestra, and that scientists were still learning who played what.

Sometimes people eat to ease boredom, sadness or loneliness, because food does comfort for a little while, and the brain has learned to rely on it. Ines said that this is deeply human, and that shame only makes the pattern harder to change, since shame is itself a painful feeling that food can soothe. If it becomes a heavy burden, she added, a doctor or counsellor can help.

Ines said that an urge to eat often rises, peaks and then fades within a matter of minutes, rather like a wave. Noor tried waiting ten minutes with a glass of water beside her, and she found that sometimes the urge faded and sometimes it did not, in which case she ate the cake and enjoyed it. That, Ines said when she heard the story, was perfectly good science and also perfectly good manners, because nobody should refuse a slice of cake out of mere duty.

On Sunday Noor and Ines went to the big supermarket on the edge of town, and Ines asked her to look at the place as a scientist might. Every surface was bright, the packets shouted in loud colours, and the air carried the smell of fresh baking from a machine near the door. Noor, who knew perfectly well that the smell was no accident, because she had once considered buying such a machine herself, felt oddly professional.

Ines pointed out that the sweetest snacks tend to sit at eye level or beside the tills, where tired shoppers and restless children cannot help but see them. Special offers and large multipacks nudge people to buy more than they planned, and the brain, which loves a bargain, does not always object. She wanted Noor to see that these are pressures from the environment, not tests of her character.

For most of human history, food was hard to find and famine was a real danger, so a body that stored energy well and enjoyed rich food may have had an advantage. Some scientists believe that we still carry those instincts into a world of plenty, though the idea is debated and probably explains only part of the story. Ines treated it as an interesting hypothesis, worth keeping in mind but certainly not a settled fact that anyone could use to excuse or accuse.

In many countries today, food is cheap, easy to obtain and available at almost any hour of the day or night, which is an extraordinary change from the world of our ancestors. Portion sizes have grown in some places, and a snack can be bought without leaving the sofa. It takes very little effort, as a result, to eat more than the body was designed to expect.

Scientists use a classification called NOVA to group foods according to how much they have been processed, and the last group, called ultra-processed, is made mostly from industrial ingredients such as flavourings, emulsifiers and refined starches. Many of these foods come in packets, last a long time and are designed to be eaten without any preparation. The category is useful, but critics note that it is broad and sometimes blunt.

In a careful but small study, twenty adults lived in a research centre for a month and spent two weeks on an ultra-processed diet and two weeks on an unprocessed one, with meals matched for sugar, fat and fibre. On the ultra-processed diet they ate about five hundred more calories a day and gained a little weight, while on the other they lost a little. It was an important experiment because it showed a difference under tightly controlled conditions.

The study was small and short, however, and it cannot tell us exactly why people ate more, whether because of speed, taste, texture or something else. Not all ultra-processed foods are alike either, and bread from a bakery may differ greatly from a factory loaf stuffed with additives. Ines said that science often advances through such cautious steps, and that the right response to a good study is interest, not panic.

Many ultra-processed foods are soft, rich and easy to swallow quickly, so a person may eat a great deal before the fullness signals have had time to arrive. Chewing, by contrast, slows the pace and gives the brakes a chance to work, though researchers are still studying how large this effect is. Noor thought of the crunch of a well-baked crust and decided that her trade might have some defence after all.

Ines reminded Noor that many people choose convenient food because they are short of money, time or energy, and that it would be unfair to blame them for what the modern shop makes easy. Cooking fresh food takes hours, skill and a kitchen, and not everybody has all three. Public health, she said, would be better served by changing the environment than by wagging a finger at individuals.

Ines suggested a few small changes to the home, such as keeping fruit where it can be seen and writing a shopping list before leaving the house. Studies of behaviour suggest that changing the surroundings often helps more than relying on willpower, though what works varies from person to person. Noor put a bowl of apples on the counter that evening, and they were gone by the end of the week.

Noor's cousin dropped into the bakery one afternoon and announced, over a cup of coffee, that she could never lose weight because she had a slow metabolism. Noor nodded sympathetically, but she realised that she had never been quite sure what the word meant. As usual, the question went to Ines, who treated it as a perfectly sensible thing to ask.

Metabolism, Ines explained, is the name for all the chemical reactions that keep a body alive, from building new cells to repairing old ones. Breathing, thinking, keeping warm and digesting a meal all use energy, and they all belong to this one enormous network of reactions. It is therefore less like a single dial that can be turned up or down than like the running costs of a very busy bakery.

Most of the energy we use each day, perhaps about half to two thirds of it, goes on simply keeping the body running at rest. This includes the beating of the heart, the work of the liver and brain and the maintenance of body temperature. Digesting food and movement use the rest, and the shares differ greatly between people, so even someone who sits all day burns a large amount just by being alive.

The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the front of the neck, and it makes hormones, among them thyroxine, that help to set the pace at which the body uses energy. Its output is controlled by the pituitary gland, a pea-sized structure under the brain that adjusts the signal as needed. Ines said she thought of it as a thermostat that keeps the whole house running at the right speed.

If the thyroid makes too little hormone, a condition called hypothyroidism, people may feel tired and cold and sometimes gain a little weight, while too much can cause a racing heart, anxiety and weight loss. Both problems can be found with a simple blood test, and both can be treated by a doctor. Ines was careful to say that such symptoms have many possible causes, so nobody should guess at the diagnosis alone.

Most people with a higher body weight, Ines said, have a thyroid that works normally, so a slow thyroid is not the usual explanation for weight, even though it is a popular one. A doctor can certainly check if there are good reasons to do so, such as other symptoms or a family history of thyroid disease. Noor's cousin, she suggested, might like to ask her doctor for a simple test, if she was worried.

People differ in how much energy they burn at rest, and most of that difference comes from the size of the body and the amount of muscle and organ tissue it contains. A smaller part of the difference is still unexplained, which means that two people of the same size can have slightly different needs. Ines emphasised that the variation is real but usually much smaller than the cousins at family parties tend to imagine.

Muscle uses somewhat more energy at rest than fat does, so a person with more muscle burns a little more over the day. The difference is modest, however, and it does not turn muscle into a magic furnace, though strength training has plenty of other benefits for the body. Ines remarked that she had met many ninety-year-olds who wished they had thought more about their muscles sooner.

When someone eats much less for a long period, the body tends to burn slightly less energy than its size would predict, a response sometimes called adaptive thermogenesis. It belongs to the same protective system that Noor had met in the garden, and falling leptin appears to be one of the signals involved. The effect is real but not enormous, and researchers are still arguing about how long it lasts.

In the supermarket Noor had seen a box of tea promising to boost your metabolism, and she held it up in the garden with a raised eyebrow. Ines laughed and said that such claims are mostly exaggerated, because the body has no single switch that a drink could turn on, and the effects of food products are usually small. Tea, she said, is lovely for plenty of other reasons, such as warmth, company and an excuse to sit down, so she poured another cup.

One morning Tariq ate three large rolls and a bowl of porridge, rubbed his stomach thoughtfully and asked whether there was anything else. Noor, who had stopped being astonished some weeks before, now began to wonder what exactly was going on in the body of a growing teenager. She did not have to wait long for an explanation, for Ines called in that afternoon.

During puberty the sex hormones, among them testosterone and oestrogen, work with growth hormone to drive a spectacular period of growth and change. Teenagers need a great deal of energy to build bone, muscle and organs, so a large appetite is normal and healthy, even when it looks alarming at the breakfast table. Ines said that Tariq's hunger was not a problem but a sign that a lot of building was under way.

Growth hormone is made in the pituitary gland and released in pulses throughout the day, with some of the biggest ones arriving during deep sleep. This is one reason why young people need plenty of rest as well as plenty of food, since the body does much of its building at night. Tariq, who liked his bed, was delighted to hear that sleeping late counted as science.

Noor's older sister Marta, who was expecting a baby in the spring, visited the bakery looking pale and a little overwhelmed. Her appetite had changed completely, and some of the smells she had always loved, including fresh bread, now made her feel sick, while other foods appeared on her wish list without warning. Noor, who had never seen her sister like this, listened closely and asked Ines about it later.

Ines explained that during pregnancy the placenta, the organ that links the mother to the baby, makes hormones of its own, among them progesterone and oestrogen. These change appetite, taste and smell, and they also make the body respond less well to insulin, which is why doctors check blood sugar during pregnancy. Needs rise only a little in the first months and rather more in the later ones.

Many women feel very hungry while they are breastfeeding, because making milk uses a considerable amount of extra energy, and the hormones prolactin and oxytocin play an important part in the process. Appetite varies a good deal between women and between different stages of feeding, and Ines said that mothers should be allowed to eat without comment. A mother's hunger is a signal worth honouring, she added, not a failure to be scolded.

Noor's mother Samira, who was in her fifties, confessed one Sunday that her sleep, her mood and her waistline had all been changing in ways she had not expected. Ines explained that during the menopause the level of oestrogen falls, and that this can affect sleep, appetite and where the body tends to store fat, although the experience differs greatly from woman to woman. Treatments exist for troublesome symptoms, she said, and a doctor can explain the options.

Men change too, Ines pointed out, and in many of them the level of testosterone drifts slowly downward with age, which may contribute to a gradual loss of muscle. Ageing varies enormously from one person to another, however, and lifestyle, illness and medicines all play their part alongside the hormones. She did not want to leave the impression that any one hormone controls the passing years.

In older people appetite often falls, and the senses of taste and smell may dim, so meals become less appealing and smaller. Ines saw this often in hospital, and she said that eating too little can become a real health problem for the elderly, with weakness and illness following in its wake. Her advice, as always, was to talk to a doctor if an older relative seemed to be losing weight without reason.

Ines summed up the week by saying that every season of life brings its own kind of hunger, and that the hormones change with the years as surely as the weather. It is therefore unfair to judge one's own body by the standards of a different age, a different sex or a different life, and nobody can hold a seventeen-year-old's appetite to a fifty-year-old's rules. Noor thought of Tariq, Marta and her mother and felt a great tenderness for all three.

Looking at an old family photograph, Noor was struck by how different her relatives were from one another, even though they had all grown up at the same table. Marta had always been tall and slender, Noor short and sturdy, and their father, in the middle, built like one of his own bread ovens. She asked Ines, when they next met in the garden, how much of all that difference could be put down to the genes.

Studies of twins, including identical twins who were brought up in different homes, suggest that genes explain a large share of the differences in body weight between people. The estimates vary, but many fall somewhere in the region of half, and nobody should treat any single figure as exact. Ines said the main message was clear enough, which is that bodies are not all built to the same pattern.

Genes do not act alone, Ines said, because they work in partnership with the surroundings in which a person lives. She compared it to two different seeds planted in the same garden bed, which will grow in different ways, but only if the soil, the water and the light allow them to. Genes may load the dice, in other words, but the environment decides how often they are thrown.

A small number of rare changes in single genes can disrupt the hunger signals in the brain, including the pathway through which leptin is read. Children who carry them can feel overwhelming hunger from a very young age, and doctors can test for some of these changes if the pattern is suggestive. Ines stressed that these cases are uncommon and that they explain only a small fraction of people.

Studies of twin children, including large ones in Britain, suggest that how strongly food captures a child's attention is partly inherited. Some children are highly responsive to food, whereas others fill up quickly and lose interest in the plate, and these traits show up early in life. Noor remembered herself and Marta at the family table, and the memory made a lot of sense.

Every person carries a different mix of bacteria in the gut, and the mix changes with diet, age, medicines and many other factors. Scientists are studying whether it affects appetite and weight, and some animal experiments hint that it might, but the research in humans is still at an early stage. Ines said that anyone selling a quick fix for the gut was, for the moment, getting ahead of the evidence.

In the winter of 1944 to 1945, a famine struck parts of the Netherlands, and food became desperately scarce for several months. Studies of people who were in the womb at that time found that those exposed to the famine early in pregnancy later had higher rates of obesity and some other health conditions. Scientists believe this shows how early life can shape the body, although the mechanisms are still under investigation.

In a well-known study from Israel, hundreds of volunteers wore sensors that measured their blood sugar after meals, including identical ones. The responses were often strikingly different from one person to the next, which shows that the same food can have different effects on different bodies. Ines took this as a warning against any diet that claims to be right for everyone.

Ines said that telling someone to just eat less ignores the enormous differences between bodies, and that it often feels like an insult to the person who hears it. Genes are not destiny, however, and habits and surroundings still make a real difference at the edges. The truth, she said, lies somewhere between blaming people for their bodies and giving up on the idea that anything can ever be changed.

Noor and Marta laughed together over the photograph, and Noor decided, quite deliberately, to stop comparing her plate with other people's. Bodies come in many shapes, she told herself, and hers had been getting her out of bed at three in the morning for years without complaint. It felt like a quiet turning point, even if nobody else in the room noticed it.

Noor remembered a strict diet she had tried at the age of twenty, in the days before she opened the bakery. She had lost some weight over three months, and then, over the following year, she had gained it all back and a little more, feeling like a failure the whole time. She asked Ines, rather shyly and without quite meeting her eye, whether the whole sorry episode had been her own fault.

Ines said that resisting hunger by willpower alone is a little like holding your breath, which anyone can do for a while but nobody can do for long. The body has powerful ways of forcing the issue, and the harder a person fights it, the stronger the pressure tends to become. Failing at that fight, she added, says nothing about someone's character and a lot about physiology.

In a well-known study of about fifty people, scientists measured hunger hormones before and after a period of rapid weight loss, and again a year later. Levels of leptin and some fullness hormones were lower, ghrelin was higher, and the volunteers reported greater appetite, and these changes had not vanished after twelve months. It does not prove that the body can never be changed, but it shows why keeping weight off is often so hard.

In 1944 and 1945, thirty-six healthy volunteers in Minnesota agreed to eat far less than usual for about six months, so that scientists could learn how to help starving people after the war. They became obsessed with food, collecting recipes and dreaming of meals, and when the experiment ended many of them ate enormous amounts for weeks. Ines told the story to show that the preoccupation with food was a normal reaction to hunger, not a sign of a weak mind.

Long-term studies show that many people regain much of the weight they lose within a few years, which is a pattern that has frustrated doctors and patients alike. Some people do succeed in keeping weight off, however, and researchers are now studying their habits and circumstances to learn what helps them. Ines said that, understood this way, regaining weight was a statistic about the body and not a verdict on anyone's willpower.

Some scientists propose that the body tries to defend a range of weight, a notion often called the set point, which would explain why lost weight so often returns after a diet. Others prefer different ideas, such as a settling point that depends on the environment, and the question is still debated among researchers. Ines said that both camps agree that the body is not a passive container.

Most researchers agree that the range a body defends is not fixed for ever, but that it may drift over the years as age, environment, sleep, illness and medicines have their effects. This helps to explain why many adults gradually gain weight over the decades, without having changed their habits as much as they think. It also leaves room for hope, since the surroundings, unlike the genes, can be changed.

Ines explained that healthier habits, such as regular walking, good sleep and plenty of vegetables, can improve fitness, blood pressure and blood sugar even when body weight barely changes. Health has many dimensions, and weight is only one of them, and it is not always the most informative. Noor was pleasantly surprised by this idea, which gave her something to aim for besides a number on the scales.

Habits still count, Ines said, because routines and surroundings can make helpful choices easier and unhelpful ones harder, and little effort is needed once a routine has settled in. Biology and habits therefore work together, and neither is the whole story, and there is no need to choose between blaming oneself and blaming one's genes. Noor wrote the word together in her notebook and drew a circle around it.

Noor felt an enormous sense of relief, for it seemed that her hunger was not a flaw in her character but a feature of her biology. Ines warned her, kindly but firmly, to be wary of anyone who sold a quick fix for such an old and complicated problem, since the honest answers are usually slow and modest. Noor, who had seen plenty of advertisements for miracle cures, promised to be careful.

Noor started work at three in the morning, when most of the town was fast asleep, and her meals fell in odd places around the clock. She asked Ines whether the time of day matters for hunger and for the way the body handles food, half hoping for a clear answer. Ines, who liked to say that biology has a clock in every room, was pleased to have been asked.

The body keeps a master clock in the hypothalamus, which is set each day by light entering the eyes, and many organs, including the liver, the pancreas and the gut, keep smaller clocks of their own. These usually follow the master clock, but food can also nudge them, so the timing of meals can influence the rhythm of the organs. The system is called the circadian clock, from Latin words meaning about a day.

In several studies, the same meal raised blood sugar more when it was eaten in the evening than when it was eaten in the morning, which suggests that the body handles sugar better earlier in the day. The effect varies from person to person, however, and it may depend on sleep, activity and the usual timing of a person's meals. Ines called it an interesting pattern and not a commandment, and she asked Noor to remember the difference.

Studies suggest that people who work night shifts have higher rates of certain health problems, including type 2 diabetes, although many factors are involved, among them light, sleep, stress and the timing of meals. Noor's early baking is not the same thing as a night shift, Ines hastened to say, and she saw no reason for alarm. The point was only that the body prefers a regular pattern when one can be arranged.

Time-restricted eating means that all of the day's food is eaten inside a window of perhaps eight to ten hours, with nothing but water or tea outside it. It has become popular in recent years, and many people say that they like the simplicity of a rule that does not involve counting anything. Ines said that popularity and proof are different things, and she wanted to look at the proof.

In many trials, intermittent fasting, including eating normally on some days and very little on others, led to about the same weight loss as ordinary calorie cutting. The evidence for extra benefits beyond that is mixed, and most of the studies so far have lasted only months or a year or two, so it is simply one option among several. Ines said that the best diet, in her experience, was the one a person could actually live with.

Ines warned that fasting is not suitable for everyone, and that children, pregnant women, people with a history of eating disorders and anyone who takes medicines for diabetes should not try it without talking to a doctor first. Frail older people also need great care, as do people with other medical conditions, and she wanted Noor to pass the warning along to anyone who asked. Health advice, she said, is only good when it fits the person receiving it.

Out of curiosity, Noor tried a long gap between meals one morning and found that by eleven she had a headache, a short temper and a flour-white face. She decided that it was not for her, and Ines said that this was a perfectly sensible result from a personal experiment, since nobody has to like something just because it is fashionable. Tariq, who had been watching her, made her a cup of tea without being asked.

Regular meals steady hunger for some people, because the body learns when to expect food, while others do better with smaller snacks spread through the day. Ines said that there is no single rule that fits everyone, and that the best pattern is the one that suits a person's body, work and family. She thought that it was more important to eat enough, and calmly, than to eat exactly on the hour.

In one small laboratory study, volunteers who ate the same meals four hours later than usual felt hungrier and burned a little less energy than when they ate early. It was a single small study, however, so more research is needed before anyone can draw firm conclusions about the effect of late eating in daily life. Ines said that this, too, was one more clue to keep in mind and not a rule to obey.

A young customer came into the bakery each week, but she never bought any bread, and she looked anxious whenever the other customers talked about food. Noor, who had been thinking about hunger for so long, was worried, and she asked Ines how to make sense of what she had seen. Ines put down her tea and said that this was an important subject, which deserved gentleness and care.

Ines explained that eating disorders, such as anorexia, bulimia and binge eating disorder, are serious medical conditions, and not choices, fads or vanity. They can affect people of any age, sex or background, they involve the mind and the body together, and effective help exists. She said that early help generally works better, so it is worth acting sooner instead of waiting for a crisis.

Signs may include constant preoccupation with food or weight, fear of eating, secrecy around meals or sudden changes in behaviour, though none of these alone proves anything. A friend can listen without judging, avoid comments about appearance and gently suggest talking to a doctor, and in many places there are helplines that offer support. Ines said that Noor should not try to be a doctor, only a kind and steady neighbour.

When the body receives too little energy for a long time, many hormones change, among them those that control growth, periods, bone strength and the response to stress. This is one reason why eating disorders can harm health in so many ways, and why recovery is so important and is possible with the right support. Ines kept her voice calm and said that nothing she described should be read as a story without hope.

Binge eating disorder involves repeated episodes of eating a large amount of food and feeling unable to stop, and it is followed by distress or shame. It is more common than many people realise and it is treatable, but the shame itself often prevents people from asking for help. Ines said that if it sounded like anyone Noor knew, the kindest first step was to mention a doctor, not a diet.

Some medicines change appetite, and some of them raise it while others lower it. Certain steroids, antidepressants and antipsychotic drugs, for example, can increase hunger, whereas some medicines for attention problems can reduce it, and nobody should ever stop taking a prescribed medicine without first talking to a doctor. Ines said that the effects vary greatly from person to person and that many people notice no change at all.

Mrs Okafor, a regular customer, confided in Noor that a new medicine had made her unusually hungry for several weeks, and that she had been ashamed of herself for eating so much. She finally told her doctor, who listened kindly and adjusted the treatment, and now she felt a great deal better. Noor thought that the story was exactly the kind Ines would have told, and she told it again that evening.

Ines said that very strong and constant hunger, together with extreme thirst, a frequent need to urinate or weight loss without trying, should be checked by a doctor as soon as possible. These can be signs of conditions that need treatment, and they should never be left to a neighbour's guess or an internet search. She repeated that she was giving general information, not advice about anyone's own body.

Low mood, long illness, pain and many other problems can change appetite, making it grow or shrink, and sometimes the change is the first sign that something else is wrong. A sudden alteration in appetite or weight that has no clear explanation deserves a conversation with a doctor, however minor it may seem. Ines said that nobody should feel they are wasting a doctor's time by asking.

Ines suggested writing down a few notes and questions before seeing a doctor, so that nothing important is forgotten in the short time available. Noor booked a routine check-up for the following week, and she felt unexpectedly proud of herself for doing something so simple and so sensible. If a doctor ever made her feel judged, Ines added, she was entitled to look for another one.

On her way to the bakery, Noor bought a plain green notebook and decided to keep it beside the till, where she could reach it between customers. For one week she would write down when she felt hungry, how strong the feeling was and what was happening around her at the time. It was not an experiment, Ines had warned, only a way of paying attention.

Each time she felt hungry, Noor gave the feeling a number from one, which meant a polite whisper, to five, which meant a shout. Beside the number she noted how well she had slept, what she had last eaten and whether the morning had been calm or rushed. By the third day the page had begun to look like a small weather chart of her own body.

When Noor read back through her first three days of notes, a pattern appeared that she had never quite noticed while living inside it. Her hunger rose most sharply at ten and at four, exactly as ghrelin's habits would suggest, and it was louder still on the mornings that followed a short night. Seeing it written down made the feeling seem less like an ambush and more like a timetable.

Ines read through the notebook with real interest, then reminded Noor that a few days of notes can suggest a pattern without proving what causes it. One person's week cannot settle large questions about hormones, she said, because too many things change at once and a single mind is a poor judge of its own mornings. Even so, a pattern was a good thing to take to a doctor, should one ever be needed.

Tariq begged to borrow the notebook for a day, and Noor agreed, half expecting him to lose it under a sack of flour. When she read his page that night, almost every number was a five, with a cheerful note beside each one about the roll or the bun that had put things right. At seventeen, Ines had said, a body that is still growing will often ask for a great deal.

On Sunday morning Noor and Ines walked briskly along the river path, and Ines used the rhythm of their steps to explain how movement affects appetite. The link exists, she said, but it is far more tangled than the posters in gyms suggest, because exercise changes several hormones at the same time and in different ways. Researchers are still working out which of those changes matter most to hunger, and nobody can yet say so with confidence.

In some studies, a bout of hard exercise lowered ghrelin and left people feeling less hungry for a short time afterwards, which surprises those who expect a workout to make everyone ravenous. Later in the day, however, appetite often catches up, and some people end up eating more than they have burned. The picture differs from person to person, and the research has not produced a simple rule.

Working muscles are able to draw glucose out of the blood, and they can do so even when only a little insulin is present, which is one reason doctors value everyday movement. Over weeks and months, regular activity also tends to help the body's cells respond better to insulin. Those benefits do not depend on a number on the scale, which is part of what makes them so encouraging.

Ines pointed out that gentle walking counts for a great deal, and that nobody needs to run marathons to give the body something useful to do. She added that exercise suits different people in different ways, and that anyone who is unwell, in pain or unsure about starting should ask a doctor first. Noor, who spent most of the day on her feet already, was pleased to hear that her kneading counted for something.

At the end of the week, Noor read through her notes once more and wrote a short list on the last page, taking care that it sounded like an invitation and not like a rulebook. She would try a proper breakfast with some protein, a few extra minutes of sleep and a walk after the shop had closed. If a change did not suit her, she would simply drop it, and that was allowed.

One morning a customer left two newspapers on the counter, and Noor was puzzled to find that their headlines blamed opposite things for weight gain. She carried both of them next door that evening and asked Ines, rather desperately, who was right. Ines laughed, poured the tea and said that this was a debate with more than one honest side.

Ines began with the part that nobody disputes, which is that the body uses energy all day long and that food is the only thing that supplies it. Over a long period, the balance between the energy consumed and the energy expended matters, since the body cannot conjure energy out of nothing. The argument, she said, starts only when people ask what pushes that balance one way or the other.

Hormones such as ghrelin, leptin and thyroid hormone touch both sides of the balance, which is why the old question of calories against hormones is a little misleading. They help to set how hungry a person feels, and they also help to set how much energy the body spends while at rest. Calories and hormones, said Ines, are not rival teams but parts of one machine.

One well-known idea, sometimes called the carbohydrate-insulin model, suggests that foods rich in carbohydrate raise insulin, and that high insulin then pushes the body to store more fat and feel hungry sooner. Some scientists support the idea, but others argue that it explains far less than its supporters claim, and the question is still being tested. Ines drew a careful question mark on the napkin beside the idea, and she left it there unanswered.

To test the idea, scientists have fed volunteers carefully controlled meals that were either low in carbohydrate or low in fat, and then measured how much energy their bodies used. The differences they found were small, and the results from different studies have not all pointed in the same direction. Ines said that when careful experts disagree like this, the sensible answer is often that the truth is more modest than the headlines.

Many different diets help some people lose weight in the short term, and studies often find that the differences between them are smaller than their fans believe. What seems to matter a great deal is whether a person can keep following the plan for months and years without misery. Ines said that a diet nobody can bear is not really a diet at all.

Ines taught Noor three questions to ask about any headline: how many people were studied, who were they, and what did the study really show beyond what the newspaper claims? A small study of a few people can offer a clue, but it can seldom provide an answer, and a single study almost never overturns what many others have found. Noor wrote the questions on the inside cover of her notebook, where she would see them whenever a new headline tempted her.

Ines reminded Noor that a finding in mice is only a first step, because a mouse is not a small person with a tail. Leptin had been dramatic in mice that could not make it, but in most people with a higher weight the story turned out to be far less simple, as Noor already knew. Good science, Ines said, often looks like a long series of careful steps and small disappointments, and patience is part of the method.

Weight is one measure of a person's health, but it is certainly not the only one, and it often hides more than it reveals. Fitness, sleep, mood, blood pressure and the results of blood tests all tell a doctor a great deal that a scale cannot, and they can be improved in many ways. Ines said that a number on its own never told anyone how well they were.

Ines said that judging people by their weight alone is both unkind and unhelpful, because it turns a complicated human being into a single number and a small insult. Research suggests that shame about weight can make people avoid doctors and cut themselves off from exercise, which is the opposite of what anyone wants. Noor thought of Mrs Okafor and of the customers who always hurried past the cakes.

On Saturday Marta brought her son Leo to the bakery for lunch, and Noor watched in amazement as the seven-year-old finished an enormous plate of pasta before anyone else had properly started. Then he asked, quite politely, whether there was any more, and whether the biscuits were allowed. Marta looked across the table with a worried expression that Noor recognised from her own childhood.

Ines told Marta that growing children need plenty of food, because their bodies are building bones, muscles and brains as well as using energy, and that a child's appetite can swing widely from one day to the next. A child should never be put on a diet unless a doctor has recommended it, she added, since the wrong kind of restriction can do real harm. It is a good moment, she said, to remember the growth spurts that Tariq had shown them.

Many experts suggest that parents offer a variety of foods at regular times and then let children decide how much to eat, instead of insisting that every plate be cleaned. This may help children to keep trusting their own hunger and fullness signals as they grow up, although families differ and no single approach suits everyone. Marta, who had always been told to finish everything, listened with her head on one side.

Over tea that evening, Ines drew the main hormones on a napkin as a relay team, with each figure passing a glowing ball to the next. Ghrelin urges the body toward food, leptin reports on the energy in store, insulin manages the fuel in the blood, and the gut hormones put a gentle brake on appetite. Noor thought that it looked a little like a child's drawing, and that this was why she could understand it.

Around the little team, Ines drew a ring of smaller figures to stand for sleep, stress, habits, genes, growth, age and the world outside the kitchen door. All of them keep turning the volume of the hormones up or down, and they help to explain why two people eating the same meal can feel quite different. Understanding hunger, she said, means listening to the whole orchestra and not to one instrument.

Ines was honest about how much science has yet to discover, including why people differ so greatly in their appetite and how the gut, the brain and the environment influence one another. Researchers are still studying how best to help people whose hunger signals work poorly, and today's firm ideas may be refined by tomorrow's studies. Noor found that this admission made her trust the rest of what she had heard even more.

When customers asked why she seemed so thoughtful, Noor told them a little of what she had learned in the garden, taking care to say that she was no expert. To her surprise, several of them offered stories of their own across the counter, about medicines, sleepless nights, strict diets and years of feeling guilty. The bakery, it seemed, had become a place where people could talk about hunger without any shame.

One morning Noor wrote a line in chalk on the board outside the shop, saying that hunger is a message and not a failure, and then she stood back to look at it. Her mother, Samira, stopped on the pavement to read it, and she smiled, squeezed her daughter's hand and went inside without a word. Noor knew that this was her mother's way of saying that she was proud.

In the garden, as the evening light faded, Noor thanked Ines for three weeks of patient explanations, and Ines accepted the thanks with a smile. She reminded Noor, as she had many times before, that she was only a retired nurse and a neighbour, and that anyone with questions about their own body should ask a doctor who knows them. Noor promised that she would book that check-up and keep asking good questions, and she meant every word of it.

Noor and Ines sat quietly in the garden as the evening light faded, and the story of hunger felt less like a puzzle and more like a conversation worth continuing. This book has offered only general information, and the science it describes is still developing, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace the care of a doctor who knows you. If you are worried about your appetite, your weight or your health, please speak to a medical professional, who can look at your own situation with the attention it deserves.
